summary: The Central African Republic lies at the center of the African continent, became independent from France in 1960, and has abundant minerals and tropical rainforest, but has long been affected by political instability.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced from the 1920s by American and European missions such as the Baptists and Lutherans, which set up churches and schools in the western and central regions. Although the French colonial authorities preferred Catholicism, the Protestant missions preached actively in rural areas and translated the Bible into Sango, so that Protestantism gained many followers. In recent decades Pentecostal and Evangelical churches have grown rapidly, making Protestants the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism began in 1894 when Spiritan missionaries established the first mission station near Bangui, and it then expanded with French colonization (the colony of Ubangi-Shari was established in 1903). In the colonial period the Catholic Church ran schools, which trained the independence leader Barthélemy Boganda, who was himself the first Catholic priest of the Central African territory. The Catholic Church also played a mediating role during the civil war, and Pope Francis visited Bangui in 2015.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to the northeast in the 19th century by merchants and slave traders from Chad and Sudan to the north, when the slave raiding of sultanates such as Wadai and Dar al-Kuti seriously affected the area. Today Muslims are concentrated mainly in the north and northeast and in the merchant community of the capital Bangui. After the mainly Muslim Séléka rebels seized power in 2013, serious fighting broke out between Muslim and Christian militias, and large numbers of Muslims were forced to flee.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs, centered on ancestor worship, nature spirits and notions of witchcraft, still have influence among the various ethnic groups. With the expansion of Christianity and Islam, those who follow only the traditional religion are a tiny minority, but many people retain traditional healing and ritual customs after converting.

religion.background: Before colonization, the Central African region had the traditional beliefs of many peoples, and the slave raiding of the northern sultanates in the 19th century brought Islam while also devastating the local population. After French colonization in the 1890s, Catholic and Protestant missionaries entered one after another and expanded their influence through schools and hospitals. After independence in 1960, Christianity became the majority religion. After the mainly Muslim Séléka coalition seized power in 2013, the mainly Christian 'anti-balaka' militias launched reprisals, religion became the dividing line of the conflict, causing heavy casualties and many refugees, and it still affects the country's peace process.

language.official: Sango and French are the official languages.

ranking.name: Sango
ranking.description: Sango was originally the language of the Sango people along the Ubangi River, became popular in the late 19th century as a lingua franca of river trade, and was also used by missionaries and the army during French colonial times, making it the country's common language. Because there are dozens of ethnic groups in the Central African Republic, Sango has become the main language of communication across ethnic lines; in 1991 it became an official language alongside French, and about 90% of the population can use it.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived when France established the colony of Ubangi-Shari in 1903; it was the language of administration and education in the colonial period and remained an official language after independence in 1960. Because the rate of schooling is low, only those with secondary education or above can use French fluently; it is mainly used in government, law and written documents, while in daily life most people use Sango.

language.history: The Central African Republic has about 70 languages, mostly of the Ubangian and Bantu families. In the late 19th century Sango began to spread as a trade language along the Ubangi River and was widely used in the army, missionary work and commerce in the French colonial period. After independence in 1960, French was the official language, but Sango continued to be the national common language. In 1991 Sango was made an official language, and the Central African Republic thus became one of the few African countries with a single indigenous language in nationwide use.

ranking.name: Gozo (cassava dough)
ranking.description: Cassava flour is poured into hot water and stirred constantly into a thick, elastic dough-like staple, with a sticky, slippery texture and mild flavor, pinched into small balls by hand and dipped in stews or sauces.
ranking.history: Cassava is native to South America and, after the 16th century, was brought to Africa by the Portuguese and then spread to the Central African region along the Congo and Ubangi river basins, becoming a main food crop because it is drought-tolerant and high-yielding. In the colonial period the French authorities also promoted cassava growing to deal with famine. Cassava dough is the most basic staple of Central African households and appears at almost every meal.

ranking.name: Ngunza (cassava leaf stew)
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded and stewed for a long time with palm oil, peanut butter, onion and dried fish or meat, with a thick texture, eaten with cassava dough.
ranking.history: Cassava leaf stew is very common in central Africa; cassava leaves are rich in protein and vitamins and are an important source of nutrition for rural families. Because cassava is widely grown locally, the leaves are cheap and easy to get and have become an important part of the daily diet. The dish is similar to the Congolese 'pondu' and 'saka-saka', reflecting the food culture shared in the Congo River basin.

ranking.name: Moambe (palm nut chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken is stewed in a thick sauce made by cooking palm fruit, with onion, garlic and chili, with a rich flavor, often served with cassava dough or rice.
ranking.history: Palm nut chicken is a traditional dish shared across central Africa and is regarded as the national dish by the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The oil palm is a plant native to the tropical rainforest of central and west Africa, and for thousands of years local people have made cooking oil and sauces from palm fruit. In the Central African Republic this dish often appears at festivals and when entertaining guests, a dish that shows sincerity.

ranking.name: Kanda (peanut butter stew)
ranking.description: A thick stew of fish or meat cooked with peanut butter, tomato and onion, with a rich, mellow texture and peanut aroma, often eaten with cassava dough.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and, after being brought to Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, were widely grown in the tropical savanna regions, becoming an important cash crop and ingredient in the Central African Republic. Peanut stew is common throughout central and west Africa, using peanuts to thicken the sauce and add nutrition. In the Central African Republic it is a dish that appears in both everyday family meals and festivals.

ranking.name: Makara (fried dough balls)
ranking.description: Dough kneaded from flour, yeast and sugar is deep-fried into puffy small round balls, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten as breakfast or a snack.
ranking.history: Fried dough balls are very common across central and west Africa under different names. Wheat flour entered the Central African region with French trade in the colonial period and gradually became an everyday ingredient for city dwellers. In cities such as Bangui, women set up stalls on the street to sell fried dough balls, an important source of family income and the most common cheap breakfast for students and office workers.
